title: Fertilizer prices surge as Strait of Hormuz disruptions tighten supply
key_claim: DAP prices rose more than 10% in April on tightening supply and sulfur costs that had doubled since January, and Morocco's OCP accelerated maintenance at its phosphate facilities in response to sulfur and ammonia disruption.
frame_summary: The World Bank is arguing that the fertiliser shock is a commodity-market event running through a shared chokepoint, and identifies sulfur, not nitrogen, as the cost driver behind the phosphate leg of it.
verbatim_quote: DAP (diammonium phosphate) prices rose more than 10 percent in April after remaining relatively stable earlier in the year. The increase reflects tightening supply conditions and rising input costs, particularly sulfur prices, which have doubled since January.
verbatim_list: Supply concerns have also intensified after Morocco's OCP accelerated maintenance at its phosphate facilities, likely in response to disruptions in sulfur and ammonia markets.
notes: Structural anchor at 95 days: the canonical primary-data statement that sulfur, not nitrogen, drives the phosphate leg. Cited inline like any other source.

publisher: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO Newsroom)
title: FAO Food Outlook: global food commodity market trends face rising geopolitical and weather risks
date_evidence: The report was published on June 18, 2026, and covers forecasts for major food commodities including cereals, oil crops, sugar, meat, dairy products, and fisheries.
key_claim: Global fertilizer trade volumes fell 20 to 25 percent between January and April 2026 against the same period a year earlier, with buying stalled in Europe and North America, particularly for nitrogen and phosphate.
frame_summary: FAO is arguing that production fundamentals remain robust but that fertiliser market disruption is the main channel through which the shock reaches the 2026/27 season.
verbatim_quote: Another chapter examines fertilizer market trends, documenting a 20 to 25 percent drop in global fertilizer trade volumes between January and April 2026 compared to the same period a year earlier.
verbatim_list: While there has been some recent abatement of rising prices, concerns remain for the upcoming 2026/27 agricultural season due to stalled buying in key markets such as Europe and North America, particularly for nitrogen and phosphate.
notes: Page body and both verbatim quotes were read off the live FAO page during sourcing. publisher: Ministere de l'Agriculture, de l'Agro-alimentaire et de la Souverainete alimentaire (France)
title: Le Gouvernement annonce un plan d'urgence engrais pour les agriculteurs et une strategie durable
key_claim: France announced emergency aid for farmers against the rise in nitrogen fertiliser prices and will support a ten-year industrial investment programme of 2 billion euros, backed by 620 million euros, to modernise and expand decarbonised nitrogen fertiliser production.
frame_summary: France is arguing that fertiliser dependency is a sovereignty problem to be solved by building domestic decarbonised nitrogen capacity, which is why the strategy contains no phosphate or sulphur feedstock measure at all.
verbatim_quote: l'État accompagnera un programme d'investissement industriel de 2 milliards d'euros sur dix ans, soutenu à hauteur de 620 millions d'euros, pour moderniser les capacités de production existantes et développer de nouvelles capacités de production d'engrais azotés décarbonés.
notes: Non-English primary source (fr). Used to evidence the policy blind spot: the whole national response is nitrogen-shaped.

title: The impact of fertilizer policies on sulphur markets
key_claim: Sulphur prices now represent around 70-80% of phosphate prices in some markets, the highest share ever recorded, and import dependence on the Middle East is concentrated: Indonesia 76%, India 84% and southern Africa 93% in 2025.
frame_summary: CRU is arguing that sulphur and phosphate have become policy-driven rather than seasonal markets, so buyers cannot solve scarcity by paying more and rationing replaces price discovery.
verbatim_quote: Sulphur prices now represent around 70–80% of phosphate prices in some markets, the highest share ever recorded.
verbatim_list: in 2025 Indonesia sourced 76% of sulphur imports from the Middle East; India depended on the region for 84% of imports; and southern Africa relied on it for 93%.
notes: Spine source for the cost-share inversion and the concentration of import dependence.

title: Metals vs fertilizers: who pays more for sulphur?
key_claim: Fertiliser is the largest-volume sulphur consumer but loses the bidding war on margin; acid is 50-60% of the cost of nickel MHP production, comparable to phosphate fertiliser, while copper, at roughly 12-18% of cathode cost, is the most aggressive bidder.
frame_summary: Kpler is arguing that the shortage is resolved by margin rather than by need, so the industry that uses the most sulphur is the one that curtails first.
verbatim_quote: The paradox is immediate: HPAL nickel is most exposed in cost terms with acid representing 50–60% of MHP production cost, comparable to phosphate fertilizers. Yet copper, where sulphur accounts for roughly 12–18% of cathode production cost, is the most aggressive bidder.
verbatim_list: By volume, fertilisers need sulphur far more than metals do. By margin and by ability to pay, they lose the bidding war.
notes: The allocation mechanism at the centre of the signal.

title: Temporary relief for markets
key_claim: Urea normalised within two weeks of the June agreement as around 820,000 tonnes on 20 vessels left the Gulf and prices returned to normal seasonal levels, but phosphate stayed high because sulphur prices did not fall.
frame_summary: CRU is arguing that the shock has two separable legs: nitrogen was a shipping problem that resolved with transit, and phosphate is a feedstock problem that did not.
verbatim_quote: Relief was most evident in urea markets, where around 820,000 tonnes of urea on 20 vessels has now been able to leave the Gulf in the two weeks (at time of writing) since the agreement, and prices have fallen to 'normal' levels for this time of year.
verbatim_list: It was a different story in phosphate markets, however, where continuing high sulphur prices have kept phosphate and hence ammonium phosphate rates high.
notes: The two-leg separation that makes the signal legible; used in the counter-counter.

publisher: East Asia Forum (Crawford School of Public Policy, Australian National University)
title: Sulphur exposes chokepoints in global production networks
key_claim: Sulphur is rarely mined directly; most global supply is recovered as a by-product of natural gas and petroleum processing, so its price and availability are tied to demand for fuels, and nearly half of world seaborne sulphur trade normally passes through the Strait of Hormuz.
frame_summary: East Asia Forum is arguing that industrial chemicals are the next frontier of supply-chain vulnerability precisely because they sit furthest upstream and their supply is set by unrelated demand.
verbatim_quote: It is rarely mined directly. Most global supply of sulphur is recovered as a by-product of natural gas and petroleum processing, and its price and availability are tied to demand for fuels.
verbatim_list: Nearly half of the world's seaborne sulphur trade normally passes through the Strait of Hormuz.
notes: Establishes the by-product structure that removes any supply response to price.

title: Global fertilizer prices are falling, African farmers aren't feeling it

key_claim: Around 640,000 tons of sulfur passed through the strait since the June deal according to Argus, and New Orleans urea barge prices fell from a wartime peak of $782 per short ton to about $350 by late June, below the pre-conflict level.
frame_summary: Ecofin Agency is arguing that the shock is a logistics and macro event already resolving, and that persistent farm-gate prices reflect currency and freight rather than any feedstock constraint.
verbatim_quote: Around 640,000 tons of sulfur, a key input for phosphate fertilizers, have passed through the strait since the June 15 deal, according to Argus.
verbatim_list: New Orleans barge prices fell from a wartime peak of $782 per short ton to about $350 by late June, below their level before the conflict began on February 28, according to StoneX data.
